title: A name that is a verb (Exodus 3:13–15)
hookLine: Moses asks God's name and hears "I AM THAT I AM"
carry: I will be what I will be

lines: I HAVE SEEN, I HAVE HEARD.
THEY WILL ASK, WHAT IS HIS NAME?
cards: From the bush, God tells Moses: I have seen the affliction of my people, I have heard their cry, and I'm sending you to Pharaoh to bring them out.
And Moses, standing barefoot on holy ground, asks a very practical question. When I tell the Israelites the God of your fathers sent me, they're going to ask: what's his name? What do I tell them?
Who are you, exactly? The answer is not quite a name.

teach.b: God answers: "I AM THAT I AM." And then: tell them, "I AM hath sent me unto you." In Hebrew: Ehyeh asher ehyeh.
Here's what an English Bible can hide.
Ehyeh is a verb, from the Hebrew root for to be, in a form that usually points forward, into the future, or into something still going on. So it can mean I am who I am. Or I will be what I will be.
Or I will be there, as I will be there. The old Jewish Publication Society translation of 1917 prints I AM THAT I AM, and notes in the margin that it could also be read I WILL BE WHAT I WILL BE.
Moses asked for a name, a label you can hold. What he got was more like a promise, and a mystery.

teach.h: I WILL BE WITH THEM IN THIS TROUBLE.
teach.b: The Talmud hears the promise: God meant, I will be with them in this trouble, and in troubles still to come. Rashi passes that on.
Other thinkers, like Maimonides, heard something about God's very being, existence itself, beyond any name. Both readings stay in the tradition.

teach.h: THE NAME TOO HOLY TO SAY.
teach.b: Then God gives one more name, made of four Hebrew letters, which tradition links to the same root: the name Jews treat as too holy to pronounce.
In prayer they say Adonai, my Lord, and in ordinary talk, HaShem, which just means the Name. This is my name forever, God says. Read the way the Talmud reads it, it doesn't say what God is.
It promises God will be there, and leaves the how open.

how: Jews do not pronounce the four-letter name of God; in prayer and Torah reading they say Adonai, and in everyday speech many say HaShem, the Name.

o: the four letters too holy to pronounce
the Lord: the title said aloud in prayer
I will be, or I am: a verb, not a title

games.q: what's inside the name — tap the pairs.
p: said in prayer, instead of the Name

s: Ehyeh is a noun, like a title
it's a verb from the root to be, often pointing to the future.
the Talmud reads it as a promise to be with the people in trouble
I will be with them in this trouble, and in troubles to come.
Jews say the four-letter name aloud in prayer
they say Adonai instead, and many say HaShem in ordinary speech.

games.q: you're Moses at the bush. you're being sent to Egypt. what's the first thing you ask about God?
games.why: he asks for the name the people will ask about. the answer is a verb: I AM THAT I AM, or I will be what I will be.

practice: Think of something you can't pin down: a question about God, about your future, about someone you love. Notice the urge to label it and settle it, then let it stay open; you don't have to know how it turns out.
If you pray, you can hold the words I will be what I will be; if not, let the question breathe with you.

wordCard.voice: Ehyeh. I will be, or I am. The name God gives Moses from the bush: a verb, a presence, and a promise.

orig.note: Hebrew: I will be what I will be, or I am that I am. from h-y-h, to be.

carryVoice: Your line: I will be what I will be. Some names are promises. See you tomorrow.

sources.q: I AM hath sent me unto you.
